newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian coffee industry appeals for tax relief.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian coffee industry appeals for tax relief.

text.p: Tanzania's coffee industry has appealed to the government for tax relief to raise farm earnings and encourage farmers to increase production.
Jeremy Lefroy of the Tanzania Coffee Association (TCA), said smallholder farmers who accounted for the bulk of production bore a disproportionate share of the state tax burden.
Lefroy is secretary of the TCA, formed in February as the dominant voice of the industry. It groups together, traders, exporters, farmers, cooperatives, agents and liquorers.
"We (the coffee industry) would like to see the tax burden at a national and local level reduced.

"Our (TCA) calculations show when you take into account the costs of producing coffee, the actual tax imposed on farmers' net incomes is very high -- 30 to 35 percent of net income after all production costs and labour," Lefroy said.
He did not give the average annual income of the local farmers but said small scale farmers were among low income earners taxed at "the highest rates in the country."

Coffee is Tanzania's agricultural mainstay with annual production for 1996/97 forecast between 41,000 to 43,000 tonnes worth about $90 million. It compares with 53,000 tonnes in the 1995/96 crop year and 55,160 tonnes average between 1981-85.
In Tanzania's northern arabica zone, about 20,000 families subsisting on small plots averaging between half and one hectare, are responsible for the bulk of coffee production.
Faced with payment problems and unpredictable returns, many farmers have uprooted their coffee trees and replanted bananas in order to raise a quick cash crop.

The TCA has already made a submission to the government for tax relief. Lefroy saw widespread bankruptcies in the industry if the Tanzanian government went ahead with a 10 to 20 percent value added tax (VAT) on exports in the 1998 financial year.
The coffee industry is not alone in complaining about Tanzania's excessive and overly bureaucratic tax system.
Finance Minister Daniel Yona has acknowledged that many complaints about the tax regime are valid and has promised a more equitable tax system in the state budget due in June.
VAT will be launched in 1998 but Yona has not said whether a VAT on exports will be included or imposed on coffee.

An example of Tanzania's so called "nuisance taxes" can be seen in the cost of locally produced coffee. Last week in Kenya, half-a-kg of premium grade Kilimanjaro coffee produced in Moshi retailed at 190 Kenyan shillings ($3.46). The same bag of coffee retailed in Moshi at the equivalent of 250 Kenyan shillings.
